title: Calcutt v. FDIC (2023)
summary: When a reviewing court finds that an agency committed legal errors in a discretionary adjudication, it must remand to the agency rather than affirm on a rationale the agency never adopted, unless the outcome on remand is certain.
notes:
Key line: "To conclude, then, that any outcome in this case is foreordained is to deny the agency the flexibility in addressing issues in the banking sector as Congress has allowed." (per curiam)

Citation: 598 U.S. 623 (2023) (per curiam).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Harry C. Calcutt III, who served from 2000 to 2013 as chief executive officer of Northwestern Bank, a community bank headquartered in Traverse City, Michigan. The respondent was the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which had ordered him removed from office, prohibited him from further participation in banking, and assessed a civil money penalty under section 8(e) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, 12 U.S.C. section 1818(e). The Solicitor General, representing the FDIC in the Supreme Court, agreed with Calcutt that the Sixth Circuit should have remanded the case to the agency after finding legal errors in the agency's decision.
sections.Material Facts: During Calcutt's tenure the bank's largest lending relationship was with the Nielson Entities, a group of 19 family owned real estate and oil businesses. On September 1, 2009, facing Great Recession losses, the Entities stopped paying their loans, then owing $38 million. A multistep arrangement called the Bedrock Transaction brought the loans current, but the Entities defaulted again on September 1, 2010, and permanently in January 2011. The FDIC opened an investigation on April 13, 2012, and on August 20, 2013, issued notices seeking to remove Calcutt and two other executives and to assess penalties, alleging mishandling and misreporting of the Nielson relationship. After a seven day hearing beginning October 29, 2019, an administrative law judge recommended a lifetime bar and a $125,000 penalty. The FDIC Board adopted that recommendation, holding that proximate cause was not required and identifying three harms: a $30,000 charge off, $6.4 million in losses on other Nielson loans, and investigative and legal expenses.
sections.Procedural History: Calcutt petitioned the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit for review of the FDIC Board's order. The Sixth Circuit agreed that the Board had misapplied the statute's by reason of requirement by holding that proximate cause was unnecessary, and it agreed in part that Calcutt had not proximately caused all of the harms the Board identified, holding him responsible for the $30,000 charge off and only part of the $6.4 million loss and treating the investigative and legal expenses as normal business costs rather than harm. Nevertheless, by a 2 to 1 vote the court affirmed the sanctions on the ground that substantial evidence supported them, reasoning that remand would be an idle and useless formality, 37 F.4th 293 (2022). Calcutt petitioned for certiorari. On May 22, 2023, the Supreme Court granted the petition limited to the first question presented and summarily reversed in a per curiam opinion.
sections.Issue: Whether a court of appeals that has identified legal errors in an agency's adjudication, here the FDIC Board's failure to apply a proximate cause standard and its reliance on harms that did not qualify under the statute, may affirm the agency's discretionary sanctions on a legal rationale the agency never adopted by conducting its own review of the record for substantial evidence, or whether the fundamental rule of administrative law stated in SEC v. Chenery Corp. and Burlington Truck Lines requires the court to remand so the agency can reconsider the case under the correct legal standard.
sections.Holding: The Court held that the Sixth Circuit erred. Reviewing courts must judge the propriety of agency action solely by the grounds invoked by the agency, and a discretionary order may be upheld only on the same basis the agency articulated. Having found two legal errors in the Board's decision, the Sixth Circuit should have remanded to the FDIC. The narrow exception for cases in which there is not the slightest uncertainty as to the outcome on remand did not apply, because whether to sanction Calcutt and how severely is a highly fact specific discretionary judgment committed to the agency, not a result the agency was required to reach. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded with instructions to remand to the FDIC.
sections.Reasoning: The per curiam opinion began with the maxim from Florida Power & Light Co. v. Lorion that when the agency has not considered all relevant factors the proper course, except in rare circumstances, is to remand for additional investigation or explanation, and that a reviewing court is not generally empowered to conduct a de novo inquiry and reach its own conclusions. Under Chenery, if the agency's grounds are inadequate the court is powerless to affirm by substituting what it considers a more adequate basis, and Smith v. Berryhill confirmed that a federal court goes astray when it decides a question delegated to an agency before the agency has addressed it. Both parties agreed the ordinary remand rule applied, and the Court cited FPC v. Idaho Power, Gonzales v. Thomas and INS v. Orlando Ventura for the principle that the reviewing court's function ends when an error of law is laid bare. The Sixth Circuit had invoked the Wyman-Gordon footnote about idle and useless formalities, but the Court has applied that exception only where the agency was required to take a particular action, as in Morgan Stanley Capital Group, so that a different rationale for a necessary result is no cause for upsetting the ruling. Sanctions under section 1818(e) are discretionary and depend on many factors bearing on culpability. To hold the outcome foreordained would deny the agency the flexibility Congress gave it.
